result: The study validated and equated subjective similarity of three shapes and three sounds through an independent experiment (n=16). Shapes were sampled from the Validated Circular Shape Space at equidistant positions, and sounds were manually generated and selected to match the shapes in subjective similarity.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C153-C156 describe a rigorous stimulus validation procedure with explicit methodology, sample size, and citation support (Li et al., 2020). The triangular geometry shown in Figure 1a provides visual confirmation of equidistant sampling, and the procedure ensures controlled baseline similarity for the main experiment.

result: Three-dimensional shape-sound objects were created by 3D-printing shapes with embedded button-activated speakers that could be manipulated to be operational or non-operational across learning days.
evaluation: Claims C5-C7 and C157-C158 describe the physical construction of experimental stimuli with detailed specifications (printer model, filament type, size). Figure 1b-c provides visual evidence of the objects and their manipulation, supporting the methodological claims.

result: A 4-day within-subject paradigm decoupled learned crossmodal object representations from baseline unimodal features. Days 1 and 3 involved behavioral exploration and similarity ratings, while Days 2 and 4 involved fMRI scanning with unimodal and crossmodal runs before and after learning.
evaluation: Claims C8-C18 describe a well-controlled longitudinal design with explicit counterbalancing (C15) and within-subject baseline (C13). Figure 2 provides comprehensive visual documentation of the paradigm structure. The design successfully isolates learning effects by controlling stimulus history and feature identity.

result: Crossmodal learning significantly changed subjective similarity ratings. Before learning, congruent and incongruent shape-sound features showed no difference in similarity (t17=0.78, p=0.44). After learning, congruent features were rated significantly more similar than incongruent features (t17=5.10, p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.28), observed in 17/18 participants and replicated in 38/44 participants.
evaluation: Claims C19-C22 and C44-C48 report robust behavioral effects with appropriate statistics (main effects, interaction, effect sizes) and high replication rate. The large effect size (d=1.28) and individual-level consistency (17/18, 38/44) provide strong evidence. Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows the data supporting these claims.

result: All participants successfully learned the shape-sound associations by the end of Day 3, achieving 100% accuracy on the learning verification task.
evaluation: Claims C42-C43 report perfect learning performance across all participants, confirming successful manipulation. While ceiling effects limit interpretation, this validates that the learning manipulation was effective and participants understood the task.

result: Whole-brain univariate analysis revealed robust bilateral modality-specific activity during unimodal runs. The ventral visual stream including perirhinal cortex showed stronger activation to visual than sound information, while the auditory processing stream including temporal pole showed stronger activation to sound than visual information.
evaluation: Claims C49-C54 describe expected modality-specific activations with appropriate whole-brain correction (voxel p=0.001, cluster p=0.05). Figure 3a-b provides visual evidence. The results replicate known neuroanatomical divisions (C53) with proper citations, establishing baseline validity.

result: Multi-echo fMRI with ICA-based denoising improved signal quality in anterior temporal regions compared to standard single-echo fMRI, addressing known susceptibility artifacts near air-tissue boundaries.
evaluation: Claims C55-C56 and C128 describe methodological advantages with visual comparison (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Claims C165-C167 and C174-C176 provide detailed acquisition and preprocessing parameters. The approach is well-justified given known limitations of standard fMRI in anterior temporal regions (C56, C127).

result: Five a priori ROIs showed modality-specific biases: perirhinal cortex (t67=5.53, p<0.001, d=0.67) and LOC (t63=16.02, p<0.001, d=2.00) were biased toward visual information, while temporal pole (t67=6.73, p<0.001, d=0.82) and A1 (t67=17.09, p<0.001, d=2.07) were biased toward sound information. V1 showed a small bias toward sound (t67=2.26, p=0.027, d=0.20).
evaluation: Claims C57-C62 report ROI-based univariate results with appropriate statistics and effect sizes. ROI definitions (C171-C173) are well-justified with citations. The V1 sound bias (C62) is unexpected but consistent with prior work (Vetter et al., 2014). Figure 3c-d shows the data.

result: Perirhinal cortex (F1,48=5.24, p=0.027, η²=0.098) and LOC (F1,45=25.89, p<0.001, η²=0.37) showed significant interactions between learning day and modality, with visual bias attenuated after crossmodal learning.
evaluation: Claims C63-C66 report learning-related changes in univariate activity with appropriate interaction statistics. The attenuation of visual bias suggests representational transformation. However, the perirhinal effect is modest (p=0.027, η²=0.098) compared to LOC, warranting cautious interpretation.

result: Temporal pole showed a significant interaction between learning day and congruency (F1,48=7.63, p=0.0081, η²=0.14). After learning, temporal pole activated more to incongruent than congruent objects (t33=2.42, p=0.021, d=0.42), while no baseline difference existed (t33=0.37, p=0.72). Other ROIs showed no congruency effects.
evaluation: Claims C67-C73 demonstrate that temporal pole differentiates learned from non-learned objects in univariate activity, controlling for unimodal features (C70). The effect is specific to temporal pole (C71-C73). Statistics are appropriate with moderate effect size (d=0.42). Figure 3d shows the data.

result: Pattern similarity analysis of unimodal feature runs revealed an interaction between learning day and congruency in temporal pole (F1,64=6.09, p=0.016, η²=0.087). After learning, congruent features showed lower pattern similarity than incongruent features (t33=3.47, p=0.0015, d=0.22), with no baseline difference (t33=0.22, p=0.82). Other ROIs showed no such interaction.
evaluation: Claims C74-C79 demonstrate learning-related changes in temporal pole pattern similarity with appropriate statistics. The finding that behavioral similarity increased while neural similarity decreased (C77) is counterintuitive but interpretable as representational transformation. Effect size is small (d=0.22) but significant. Figure 4 shows the data.

result: Before crossmodal learning, all ROIs showed modality-specific pattern similarity biases. Temporal pole (F1,32=15.80, p<0.001, η²=0.33) and A1 (F1,32=145.73, p<0.001, η²=0.82) showed greater similarity for matching sound features, while perirhinal cortex (F1,32=10.99, p=0.0023, η²=0.26), LOC (F1,30=20.09, p<0.001, η²=0.40), and V1 (F1,32=22.02, p<0.001, η²=0.41) showed greater similarity for matching visual features.
evaluation: Claims C80-C85 establish baseline modality-specific biases in pattern similarity with strong statistics and large effect sizes (especially A1: η²=0.82). This provides the foundation for assessing learning-related changes. The analysis appropriately correlates unimodal features with crossmodal objects.

result: After crossmodal learning, perirhinal cortex was no longer biased toward visual shape (F1,32=0.12, p=0.73), while other ROIs maintained their modality biases (F1,30-32 between 16.20 and 73.42, all p<0.001). The interaction between learning day and modality in perirhinal cortex was significant (F1,775=5.56, p=0.019, η²=0.071), indicating attenuation of the baseline visual bias.
evaluation: Claims C86-C93 demonstrate unique transformation of perirhinal cortex representations with appropriate statistics. The loss of visual bias (C86, C92) and significant interaction (C88) support abstraction from unimodal features. However, the effect size is modest (η²=0.071), and the large df (775) suggests pooling across conditions. Figure 5 shows the data.

result: Cross-day pattern similarity analysis revealed that perirhinal cortex was the only region differentiating congruent from incongruent objects (F1,34=4.67, p=0.038, η²=0.12). Pattern similarity did not differ from zero for congruent objects (t35=0.39, p=0.70) but was significantly below zero for incongruent objects (t35=2.63, p=0.013, d=0.44). Other ROIs showed significant positive correlations across days without congruency effects.
evaluation: Claims C94-C100 demonstrate that perirhinal cortex representations were transformed after learning (C100) while differentiating object types (C99). The pattern of results (congruent=0, incongruent<0) is consistent with pattern separation (C113-C114). Statistics are appropriate, though the congruency effect is modest (p=0.038). Figure 6 shows the data.

result: Temporal pole and perirhinal cortex came to represent crossmodal object concepts that differed from constituent unimodal features. Perirhinal cortex showed initial visual bias that was attenuated with experience, with acquired object concepts becoming less similar to original unimodal features, consistent with integrative coding different from the sum of component parts.
evaluation: Claims C101-C105 synthesize findings from multiple analyses (Figures 4-6) into a coherent interpretation. The evidence supports integrative coding in anterior temporal lobes (C105) and abstraction in perirhinal cortex (C103-C104). However, C104 includes speculative interpretation about mechanisms of abstraction that goes beyond the data.

result: Hippocampus and inferior parietal lobes showed convergence of unimodal feature representations (sensitivity to both visual and sound features) but no evidence of crossmodal integrative coding different from unimodal features. These regions did not differentiate congruent from incongruent conditions or change with experience.
evaluation: Claims C147-C150 report null results for exploratory ROIs with appropriate statistical tests. The distinction between convergence (C147) and integrative coding (C148) is conceptually important. Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows the data. The null results are interpretable given the controlled design.

result: The study proposes that temporal pole and perirhinal cortex may be involved in integrative coding through different mechanisms. Temporal pole may combine previously learned knowledge (conceptual combination), while perirhinal cortex may perform pattern separation. However, the exact nature of the integrative code remains an open question.
evaluation: Claims C106-C116 are largely speculative interpretations (C106, C110, C112-C116 marked as SPECULATION). While the differential patterns in temporal pole (C108-C109) and perirhinal cortex support distinct mechanisms, alternative explanations exist (C115-C116). The conceptual combination interpretation (C110-C111) and pattern separation interpretation (C112-C114) are plausible but not definitively established.

result: The study found that temporal pole and perirhinal cortex represent crossmodal objects after a period of learning, consistent with animal research. The study explicitly controlled stimulus history, potentially explaining mixed findings in prior literature. However, whether effects are driven by experience alone or combined with sleep-dependent consolidation remains unclear.
evaluation: Claims C117-C122 appropriately contextualize findings with prior work (C118, C121) and acknowledge limitations (C119). The explicit control of stimulus history (C122) is a methodological strength. However, C119 identifies an important confound (experience vs. consolidation) that cannot be resolved with the current design.

result: Temporal pole and perirhinal cortex differentiated learned from non-learned crossmodal objects while controlling for unimodal features, providing evidence for integrated crossmodal object representations different from unimodal features. Perirhinal cortex showed initial visual bias that was attenuated by learning, potentially representing a mechanism for conceptual abstraction.
evaluation: Claims C23-C28 summarize the main findings from the abstract. These are well-supported by the detailed results (C67-C100). However, C28 is speculative about mechanisms of abstraction. The claims appropriately emphasize the key experimental control (same unimodal features for congruent/incongruent objects).

result: The introduction establishes that crossmodal integration is essential for object recognition and concept learning, but the crossmodal binding problem remains poorly understood. Current AI systems struggle with crossmodal integration, potentially due to inability to resolve the binding problem. Theoretical views differ on whether crossmodal objects are built from distributed features or involve integrative coding in anterior temporal lobes.
evaluation: Claims C29-C41 provide appropriate background with extensive citations. The characterization of theoretical debates (C37-C39) and AI limitations (C35-C36) is well-supported. The critique of prior literature focusing on visual domain alone (C40) justifies the current study's crossmodal approach.

result: The study applied multi-echo fMRI across a 4-day paradigm that decoupled learned crossmodal object representations from baseline unimodal features, allowing tracking of crossmodal object representation emergence in healthy adults.
evaluation: Claims C32-C34 accurately describe the methodological approach. The decoupling of learned objects from baseline features (C33) is the key innovation enabling the main findings. The claims are supported by detailed methods (C8-C18, C165-C167).

result: The findings complement patient work linking anterior temporal lobe damage to concept loss by showing that formation of new crossmodal concepts recruits these structures. The anterior temporal lobe may contain 34 distinct functional regions, suggesting greater complexity than simple temporal pole vs. perirhinal cortex divisions. Multi-echo fMRI addresses known signal dropout challenges in this region.
evaluation: Claims C123-C128 appropriately contextualize findings with clinical literature (C123) and acknowledge complexity (C125-C126). The methodological contribution of multi-echo fMRI (C128) is well-supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1. C126 appropriately notes limitations of the current ROI approach.

result: The study proposes that perirhinal cortex may be by default visually driven as an extension of the ventral visual stream but can act as a polymodal hub after learning. Alternative explanations include sensitivity to tactile information from visual features. LOC also showed reduced visual bias, possibly reflecting visual imagery or feedback connectivity, but perirhinal cortex was unique in complete attenuation of visual bias.
evaluation: Claims C129-C134 are largely speculative interpretations (C129-C131, C133 marked as SPECULATION). While the data support attenuation of visual bias in perirhinal cortex (C134, supported by C86-C93), the mechanistic explanations (hub function, tactile sensitivity, feedback connectivity) are not directly tested. Multiple plausible interpretations exist.

result: The findings relate to prior work showing anterior temporal lobes are important for configural representations, with perirhinal damage causing discrimination impairments. Similar errors occur in deep learning models, potentially due to inability to resolve the binding problem. Future work mimicking anterior temporal lobe coding properties may improve AI systems.
evaluation: Claims C135-C141 appropriately connect findings to clinical literature (C135-C137) and AI research (C138-C140). The parallel between patient deficits and AI errors (C138-C139) is well-cited. However, C141 is speculative about future AI applications, though reasonably grounded in the findings.

result: The perirhinal cortex mask overlaps with the proposed hub region in the 'hub and spokes' model. While prior work has linked hippocampus and inferior parietal lobes to convergence of unimodal representations, this work often does not differentiate between convergence and integrative coding, nor control for stimulus-based factors.
evaluation: Claims C142-C146 appropriately position findings within theoretical frameworks (C142) and critique prior literature (C145-C146). The distinction between convergence and integrative coding (C145) is conceptually important and justified by the current findings (C147-C150).

result: The study concludes that forming crossmodal object concepts relies on representations for whole objects in anterior temporal lobes that differ from distributed unimodal features in sensory regions. This hierarchical architecture supports understanding of the external world and provides one solution to the crossmodal binding problem.
evaluation: Claims C151-C152 appropriately summarize the main conclusions. The hierarchical architecture claim (C152) is supported by the distributed findings across ROIs. However, the claim of providing 'one solution' to the binding problem is somewhat overstated given remaining mechanistic uncertainties (C106, C115-C116).

result: Twenty participants were recruited for the main study, with two excluded (one dropout, one artifact), resulting in 16-17 participants in final analyses depending on data availability. Participants were right-handed with normal vision/hearing and no psychiatric history. Compensation was $250 CAD plus $50 completion bonus.
evaluation: Claims C159-C164 provide transparent reporting of sample size, exclusions, and demographics. The final sample size (16-17) is modest for fMRI but appropriate for the within-subject design with multiple measurements per participant. Exclusion criteria are clearly stated.

result: The study used a psychophysics-inspired approach with many repetitions of the same stimuli (40 instances per unimodal feature, 20 instances per crossmodal object per session) in 3-minute 'mini-runs'. Single-trial estimates used the least squares single approach with 2mm smoothing, and pattern similarity used z-transformed Pearson correlations.
evaluation: Claims C168-C170 and C177-C178 describe appropriate methods for multivariate pattern analysis with proper citations (Coutanche & Thompson-Schill, 2012; Mumford et al., 2014). The high number of repetitions (C168-C169) provides good power for pattern analysis. The 3-minute runs (C170) are justified for improving data quality.

result: A behavioral replication with 44 new participants confirmed the learning-related shift in pattern similarity, observed in 38/44 participants.
evaluation: Claims C179 and C22 report a successful replication with larger sample size. The high replication rate (38/44 = 86%) is consistent with the original finding (17/18 = 94%), providing strong evidence for the robustness of the behavioral effect.
